One-page brief for the Director of Customer Experience

Bottom line: Customers mostly complain about how they are treated when things go wrong, not only about the delays themselves. Software can read tweets well enough to triage, not well enough to replace your reading team.

1. What are customers saying?

  • 63% of tweets are negative (Twitter over-represents unhappy customers). Top complaint reasons: Customer Service Issue (32%), Late Flight (18%), Can't Tell (13%).
  • Phrases that name the problem: customer service + hold/call back, cancelled flight(led), lost bag, hours late. Praise is short and about people: thanks, crew, agents.

2. Can software replace manual reading?

  • A standard sentiment tool agrees with human labels 55% of the time (always-guessing 'negative' gets 63%); it misses 49% of truly negative tweets - largest single cause of disagreement: lexicon false alarm (politeness/positive word in neutral tweet); airline words (delayed, cancelled, lost) and sarcasm are also misread.
  • Adding an airline vocabulary lifts agreement to 60% and negative recall to 60%. Humans themselves disagree on part of the labels, so ~100% is not a realistic goal.
  • Recommendation: automate the first pass and the triage; keep people for urgent, mixed and uncertain tweets.

3. How do we compare, and where do we act first?

  • Complaint mixes differ significantly by airline (Cramer's V 0.11, small-to-moderate). Highest customer-service share: American; highest operations share: Delta. The clean 'one airline = service, another = operations' story is only partly supported.
  • Highest negative share: US Airways (78%); most tweets: United. Report shares with raw volume beside them; Virgin America is too small (n=504) to rank confidently.
  • Negative share varies by day (peak 2015-02-22), but the data cannot say why - link it to operations data.

Actions, in order

  1. Fix the response, not just the flight: hold times / call-backs / rebooking for cancelled flights - the largest complaint block.
  2. Triage rule: reply to P1 within 30 min (stranding/loss/cancellation language, churn threats, already retweeted, competitor named) - only 8% of negatives (739 tweets).
  3. Deploy the domain-adapted sentiment tool as a first pass, audit 100 tweets a week, retrain quarterly.
  4. Count customers, not tweets: link repeat complaints into one case and escalate the second one.
  5. Use staff language: route named-staff praise to recognition and named-staff complaints to coaching.

Confidence and limits: single 9-day window in Feb 2015, Twitter users only, crowd-sourced labels. Most solid: complaint types and tool weaknesses. Least solid: why complaints spike on a given day, and small-airline rankings. Today's data would change the airline list, vocabulary and platform mix.

Reading: on the 4,864 tweets that contain a negation, accuracy is 0.546 on raw text vs 0.416 after standard stop-word removal vs 0.539 with our list; overall accuracy barely moves (it does not reliably improve either), because VADER relies on punctuation, capitals and word order that stop-word removal damages. Meaning is the bigger problem: 'that's not good enough' becomes 'that's good' (table above). Rule used in this lab: score sentiment on RAW text; use the stop-word-filtered text only for counting words.

Why raw frequency fails: the top words (thanks, customer, service, hold, time...) occur in BOTH groups, so their counts barely differ between classes; Zipf's law means a few common words dominate every list. Operational insight a single word hides: 'service' alone is ambiguous (praised AND criticised) but 'customer service' + 'hold'/'call back'/'no response' point at call-centre responsiveness; 'cancelled flight(led)' is a re-booking/compensation problem; 'lost bag' is baggage handling. 'Late' alone could be a delay or a compliment ('not late'). Sentiment flips: 'good' is positive but 'not good' is overwhelmingly negative; 'problem' is negative but 'no problem' is positive/neutral - exactly what unigram counts and standard stop-word lists destroy.

B4. Word cloud vs bar chart

I would show the BAR CHART to the Director. A word cloud encodes count as font size, but readers perceive AREA and word length (long words look bigger), position is random, and counts such as 'delay' (917) vs 'customer' (780) cannot be compared precisely by eye - it gives a vague 'it is all about service and time' impression. The bar chart is ordered, has a common baseline, exact numbers and supports decisions. Use the cloud only as a decorative cover image to set the theme.

C3. Three tweets where counting words misleads the tool

My own adversarial tweets
tweet VADER score tool says my human label with airline lexicon
@united Great, another cancelled flight. Thanks for ruining my honeymoon, you're the best! +0.91 positive negative positive
@AmericanAir Stuck on the tarmac for 4 hours, bags lost, rebooked twice and nobody has called back. -0.51 negative negative negative
@Delta The crew killed it today, absolutely crushed the turbulence, hell of a flight - not bad at all! -0.89 negative positive negative
  • Tweet 1 - SARCASM: 'Great', 'Thanks', 'best' are strongly positive in the lexicon; the sentence is a complaint. Bag-of-words cannot see that praise is aimed at the opposite of its meaning.
  • Tweet 2 - NO SENTIMENT WORDS / DOMAIN VOCABULARY: every word describes a bad situation (stuck, lost, hours, rebooked) but none is an 'emotion word' in a general lexicon, so the score is ~neutral. The facts carry the sentiment.
  • Tweet 3 - SLANG + NEGATION: 'killed', 'crushed', 'hell' are negative in the lexicon but are positive slang here; 'not bad' is a negated negative. Counting word polarities gives the wrong direction.

Keeping only fully-agreed labels (confidence = 1.0, 71.3% of the data) moves accuracy from 0.550 to 0.596 (+0.046) and macro-F1 from 0.514 to 0.535; the share of negatives changes from 63% to 71%. Part of the 'tool errors' were human disagreement; the confidence column is the share of crowd-workers who agreed, so 29% of tweets have contested labels (mostly neutral/mixed ones). Why it matters: the 'ground truth' is itself a noisy human judgement, so accuracy has an error bar coming from the labels, and a model can never be judged to 100% of a target that humans only agree on partially. Report results on both the full and the high-confidence set.

RULE (scored, explainable, uses only information the airline has in real time): +2 safety/stranding/loss/cancellation language (stranded, tarmac, lost, cancelled, kids, medical...); +2 churn or escalation language (never again, worst, lawyer, 'complaint'); +2 the tweet has already been retweeted (public amplification); +1 each for a stated duration in hours, a money/refund claim, a second airline handle (competitor risk), a very negative score, SHOUTING/!!!. P1 = 4+ points, P2 = 2-3, P3 = rest; labels with confidence < 0.6 never reach P1/P2 automatically (human check first). Why: it ranks by (a) harm to the customer, (b) reputational reach and (c) churn risk, not by how angry the words sound - sentiment strength alone would push sarcasm and swearing to the top and bury calm, serious cases ('stuck 6 hours, my medication is in the checked bag'). It keeps the first-response queue manageable: only 8.1% of negatives are P1. Limits: weights are judgement-based and should be calibrated against real outcomes (escalations, refunds, churn).

PART E - Limits of the data

E1. Three (or more) ways this dataset can mislead

  • Self-selection / negativity bias: people tweet when something went wrong - 62.7% of tweets are negative, which says nothing about how most passengers feel. Silent satisfied passengers and non-Twitter users are invisible.
  • Query-based sampling frame: tweets were collected by searching for airline handles, so only people who tagged the airline appear; complaints about an airline that do not tag it are missed, and airline-name frequencies mean nothing (B1).
  • Demographic / geographic skew: Twitter users skew younger and urban, the data is US-only, and only 7.0% of tweets have coordinates and 67.7% a location - we cannot check who is represented.
  • Non-independence: 3,000 users tweet more than once (top user: 63 tweets) - a few vocal customers can inflate a complaint category; bots/templated replies and retweets add duplicates.
  • Label noise and tiny gold set: the labels come from crowd workers (confidence mean 0.90); only 40 'gold' labels exist.
  • Different airlines have different customer bases, social-media habits and customer-care teams that actively monitor Twitter (more complaints get posted where a response is likely).

Which finding I trust LEAST: the day-by-day 'why' (D3: 9 days, 2 partial, no cause variables) and any single-airline claim for the smallest airline (Virgin America, n=504); cross-airline share comparisons (D1/D2) are second-least trustworthy because of different tweeting habits per airline. The ranking of complaint TYPES overall and the VADER error analysis are the most solid.

E2. What would change with data from today?

  • Platform and users: Twitter is now X; the user base, tweeting habits, bot share and API access changed, so volume, negativity and demographic skew would all differ.
  • Airlines: Virgin America no longer exists as a brand (merged into Alaska); US Airways merged into American; ULCCs (Spirit, Frontier) and JetBlue now dominate complaint volume - the airline comparison (D1/D2) would change completely.
  • Complaint vocabulary: 'basic economy', app/check-in glitches, seat-selection fees, wifi, DM-for-help, and post-pandemic refund/credit/vouchers and staffing shortages would appear; 'flightled' (2015 jargon) would fade.
  • Language: emoji, GIFs, memes, images-as-text and new slang would be common - a 2015 lexicon (VADER's emoji list, sarcasm markers) ages quickly; modern transformer models would handle context better.
  • Probably STABLE: the dominance of customer-service and delay/cancellation complaints, the negation/sarcasm failure modes of lexicons, the heavy-tailed word distribution and the need to look at shares rather than counts.

E3. Should the manual tweet-reading team be replaced?

Argument AGAINST full replacement (recommended: HYBRID). The tool agrees with humans only 55.0% of the time (kappa 0.32); it misses 49.0% of truly negative tweets - the ones the airline most needs to catch - and its main failure modes (airline jargon, sarcasm, negation, slang) are systematic, not random. It also cannot judge urgency or give the 'why'. Argument FOR automation: it is instant (the problem today is that humans react days late), consistent, free per tweet, strong on clear positive/negative language, and perfect for volume dashboards. Recommendation: automate the first pass (score + route + triage tier from D4, domain-adapted lexicon -> accuracy 60.2%), keep humans for P1/P2, low-confidence and neutral/'mixed' cases, sample 100 tweets/week for human audit, and re-train/re-validate quarterly. Replace the READING, not the READERS.

PART F - Additional insights

Insight 1
Observation Neutral tweets are mostly questions and requests, not 'no opinion' - they are unanswered service demand.
Evidence 39% of neutral tweets contain a question mark vs 26% of negative and 4% of positive tweets.
Why it matters Unanswered questions (rebooking rules, baggage, status) turn into negative tweets later, and they are the cheapest tweets to resolve with a template or a chatbot.
Recommended action Auto-detect questions ('?', how/can/when) and route them to a self-service/FAQ flow so staff time goes to P1/P2 complaints.
Confidence and limits Medium: '?' also appears in rhetorical complaints ('why is my flight late again?').
Insight 2
Observation A measurable group of tweets mentions two or more airlines - a customer comparing you with a competitor or rebooking onto one.
Evidence 486 tweets (3.3%) contain 2+ airline handles; 77.0% of them are negative vs 62.7% overall.
Why it matters These customers are shopping alternatives; a negative tweet naming a competitor is an immediate churn risk.
Recommended action Add 'competitor named' to the triage score (done in D4) and track it as a share-of-voice KPI.
Confidence and limits Medium: multi-handle tweets include replies in conversations and 'thanks @A and @B' co-mentions.
Insight 3
Observation A large part of the negative volume comes from users who complain more than once.
Evidence 3,100 users tweeted one negative tweet; 1,873 users sent 2+ and account for 66.2% of all negative tweets; the most active user posted 28 negatives.
Why it matters Counting tweets overstates how many customers are unhappy; an unresolved case generates several tweets and signals a failed first response.
Recommended action Count unique customers, link follow-ups into one case, and flag 'second negative tweet from the same user in 48 h' as an escalation.
Confidence and limits Medium: the user 'name' is a handle, not a verified identity; some repeats are accounts with several incidents.
Insight 4
Observation Public reach is extremely concentrated: a tiny number of tweets get all the retweets.
Evidence Only 5.2% of tweets were retweeted; the top 1% of tweets hold 48.7% of all retweets; share retweeted: negative 6.5%, neutral 3.0%, positive 3.2%.
Why it matters Reputation damage comes from a few viral complaints; most tweets reach only the airline.
Recommended action Monitor retweets/likes in real time and move a tweet to P1 as soon as it starts to spread (D4 gives retweeted tweets +2).
Confidence and limits Medium: retweet_count is a 2015 snapshot at collection time, so recent tweets have had less time to spread.
Insight 5
Observation Negative tweets are longer than positive and neutral ones - complaints are explanations, praise is a one-liner.
Evidence Mean words per tweet: negative 18.6, neutral 13.2, positive 12.8.
Why it matters Length is a free, language-independent signal of a detailed complaint with context worth reading; it also explains why short tweets ('thanks!') are easy for lexicons and long ones are hard.
Recommended action Add length as a triage feature and route long negative tweets to human reading first.
Confidence and limits Medium-high: effect is clear but modest; 140-character cap compresses differences.
Insight 6
Observation The negative share is not constant through the day.
Evidence Highest negative share around 0:00 (74%), lowest around 10:00 (56%) by the tweet's timestamp (Pacific, -0800).
Why it matters Staffing the social-care desk uniformly wastes capacity; complaint intensity has a daily rhythm that follows travel disruptions.
Recommended action Staff the response team by hour using this curve and check it again with more weeks of data.
Confidence and limits Low-medium: 9 days only; hours are in one timezone while customers are across the US.

Insight tags

Insights 1-6 above go beyond the 20 statements: neutral tweets as unanswered questions, competitor mentions, repeat complainers, amplification concentration, tweet length and hour-of-day rhythm.
